title: Perturbative Renormalization of Noether Currents in SYM with Improved Discretizations
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, Contribution to the 43rd International Symposium on Lattice Field Theory (Lattice 2026)
summary: We investigate the perturbative renormalization of Noether currents associated with chiral symmetry and supersymmetry transformations in $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, regularized on the lattice using improved discretizations. In particular, we study the chiral current and the supercurrent operator for a broad class of lattice actions: Wilson fermions with one-step stout-smeared links and a clover term, together with a family of Symanzik-improved gluon actions. Since the supercurrent mixes with both gauge-invariant and gauge-noninvariant operators, we compute the corresponding renormalization factors and mixing coefficients at one-loop order. We analyze the impact of improved gluon and gluino actions on this mixing pattern and investigate whether suitable choices of lattice parameters, such as the clover and stout coefficients, can reduce unwanted lattice artifacts at one loop. Our results provide perturbative input for the implementation of Ward identities and for matching lattice observables to their continuum counterparts, while also offering guidance for simulations aimed at restoring supersymmetry in the continuum limit.

title: Impact of Window Observables on the Transversity Quark Parton Distribution Function
summary: We study the potential impact of lattice QCD window observables on nucleon isovector quark transversity parton distribution functions (PDFs) using the ePump Hessian-updating framework. Window observables, recently proposed in arXiv:2505.22795 as benchmark quantities enabling direct quantitative comparison between lattice QCD and phenomenological PDF extractions, are weighted integrals of PDFs over a range of Bjorken-$x$ for which both approaches are reliable. Experimental determinations of transversity PDFs carry uncertainties of 50--100%, while current lattice calculations have achieved comparable or better precision, creating an opportunity for lattice inputs to significantly constrain a global analysis. We evaluate the constraining power of existing lattice QCD computations of transversity window moments and Gaussian windows against current phenomenological PDF. We additionally examine prospective tensor charges in the transversity channel and estimate the PDF uncertainty reduction achievable at current and near-future lattice precision. Our results provide quantitative guidance on which window observables will most constrain global PDF analyses.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the impact of lattice QCD window observables on nucleon isovector quark transversity PDFs using the ePump Hessian-updating framework, showing that current and near-future lattice calculations can significantly reduce uncertainties in global PDF analyses.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to explore how lattice QCD window observables can improve the precision of transversity parton distribution functions (PDFs), given that existing experimental determinations have large uncertainties and lattice calculations are achieving comparable or better precision, thus potentially providing stronger constraints for a global analysis.
AI.method: The method involves evaluating the constraining power of existing lattice QCD computations of transversity window moments and Gaussian windows against current phenomenological PDFs, as well as examining prospective tensor charges in the transversity channel, using the ePump Hessian-updating framework.
AI.result: The results indicate that certain window observables, particularly from current and near-future lattice QCD calculations, can significantly constrain global PDF analyses, thereby reducing the uncertainty in the transversity PDFs.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that specific lattice QCD window observables offer significant potential for improving the accuracy of global PDF analyses, with particular emphasis on the role of current and future lattice precision in this improvement.

title: Time-Domain Observables for Resonant Scattering in Quantum Simulations of Lattice Gauge Theory
summary: Quantum computing may allow unprecedented access to nonequilibrium quantum dynamics, including problems of interest in particle physics, like the real-time development of scattering processes. Although fault-tolerant simulations at scale are still in the future, recent advancements toward early fault-tolerant simulations motivate building increasingly elaborate benchmark problems in order to assess state-of-the-art capabilities and test new algorithms and observables. In this work, we study glueball scattering on a line-of-plaquettes lattice in pure $SU(3)$ lattice gauge theory. We characterize scattering of the lowest-energy glueball states using classical exact diagonalization methods, identifying the continuum resonance structure using real-time simulations and approximate analytic methods, and we propose time-domain observables for extracting properties of the resonance from quantum simulations. We furthermore construct a toy model that shares the spectral features of the lattice gauge theory and demonstrate extraction of the observables. Feasibility on near-term hardware is demonstrated through simulation of a resonant collision of this toy model on Quantinuum System Model $\texttt{H2-2}$, with a 14-plaquette chain encoded in 28 qubits. The Trotterized circuit after optimization and compression requires $\sim 25n$ entangling gates for $n$ Trotter steps.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the simulation of glueball scattering in quantum computing, using a line-of-plaquettes lattice and $SU(3)$ lattice gauge theory. The authors employ classical exact diagonalization and analytic methods to characterize the scattering, propose time-domain observables for resonance properties, and validate their approach on near-term quantum hardware with a 14-plaquette chain encoded in 28 qubits.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to assess current quantum computing capabilities for simulating complex nonequilibrium quantum dynamics, such as glueball scattering, and to prepare for future fault-tolerant simulations by creating benchmark problems that can test new algorithms and observables.
AI.method: The method involves characterizing the scattering of lowest-energy glueball states through classical exact diagonalization, identifying continuum resonance structure, and proposing time-domain observables. A toy model sharing spectral features with the lattice gauge theory is constructed, and the feasibility of the approach is demonstrated on Quantinuum's System Model H2-2 with a 14-plaquette chain and 28 qubits, using a Trotterized circuit requiring approximately 25n entangling gates for n Trotter steps.
AI.result: The results include the successful characterization of glueball scattering, identification of resonance structures, and the proposal of new time-domain observables. Additionally, the authors show that it is feasible to simulate the toy model on near-term quantum hardware, which supports the potential for further exploration of quantum simulations of particle physics phenomena.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that it is possible to simulate and analyze glueball scattering using quantum computing, even on near-term devices, by employing specific models and optimized circuits. This work provides a stepping stone for more advanced simulations and the development of quantum algorithms for particle physics research.

title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
summary: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(φ^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the use of diffusion models, trained using a target score identity with unnormalized probability density, for generating independent field configurations in lattice field theory. The method avoids the need for samples from the target distribution and performs comparably to traditional HMC data training across different phases of 2D φ⁴ theory.
AI.motivation: The motivation behind this research is to address the significant computational challenge in lattice field theory, which is the sampling of equilibrium field configurations. The aim is to develop generative samplers capable of producing independent configurations, thus potentially overcoming the bottleneck that hinders progress in the field.
AI.method: The authors employ diffusion models but adapt their training by utilizing the target score identity and the unnormalized probability density, rather than relying on the standard denoising score matching that requires target distribution samples. They also explore both importance-weighted and unweighted versions of the identity to maintain consistency during training and to establish a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme.
AI.result: The results show that the proposed data-free training approach for diffusion models is effective and efficient, as it allows for successful training and sampling in various phases (symmetric, critical, and broken) of 2D φ⁴ theory. The performance achieved is on par with that obtained when training on reference data generated by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC).
AI.conclusion: The conclusion drawn from this study is that diffusion models can be effectively trained without the need for pre-existing samples from the target distribution, by leveraging the target score identity. This novel training approach not only circumvents the original sampling problem but also demonstrates comparable performance to conventional methods, suggesting a promising direction for generative sampling in lattice field theory.
